findings.claim: `DIRTY_MOCK_STATES.add.bind(...)` produces a function whose return value is the Set itself, not `void`; if `addDirtyMock` is handed to a callback slot that consumes the return value, the Set leaks into that value.
findings.rationale: `Set.prototype.add` returns the set for chaining. A bound alias named like a void-returning notifier (`addDirtyMock`) is very likely passed as a callback (e.g. stored on the mock state, `.then(addDirtyMock)`, `.map(addDirtyMock)`). In any of those positions the returned `Set<Mock<...>>` becomes the produced value instead of `undefined`, which can surprise the consumer. TypeScript will not flag it because a non-void return is assignable to a `void`-returning signature. Wrapping it (`const addDirtyMock = (m) => { DIRTY_MOCK_STATES.add(m) }`) removes the hazard. Moderate confidence — depends on the call sites not shown in this hunk.

findings.claim: Exposing a bound `add` handle lets arbitrary callers insert mocks into `DIRTY_MOCK_STATES`, which holds strong references and therefore defeats the WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry memory strategy used for `REGISTERED_MOCKS` right below it.
findings.rationale: `REGISTERED_MOCKS` deliberately uses `WeakRef` + `FinalizationRegistry` so mocks can be collected. `DIRTY_MOCK_STATES` is a plain `Set` holding strong refs; anything added stays alive until something explicitly clears it. Creating a detached, freely-passable `addDirtyMock` widens the set of places that can pin mocks in memory (and it cannot be paired with a finalizer since the handle carries no removal counterpart). If this alias is handed out to per-mock state objects, mocks that are never `mockClear`ed will never be collected. Confidence is moderate: the leak risk is pre-existing, but this change makes the insertion path easier to spread.

findings.claim: The bound alias is created eagerly at module evaluation time and permanently captures the current `DIRTY_MOCK_STATES` instance, so any future reassignment or test-time replacement of the set would silently be ignored by `addDirtyMock`.
findings.rationale: `DIRTY_MOCK_STATES` is `const` today, so this is safe as written, but the bound reference is a hidden coupling: if someone later swaps the set (e.g. to reset global state between test files, a common need in a mocking package), writes through `addDirtyMock` would still target the stale set while reads go to the new one. Low confidence that this is a live bug; flagging as a fragility introduced by the binding.
